name: Citrine
lede: Citrine is a lemon-to-greenish yellow named for the citron, the color of the yellow quartz, and an old artists' word for a muddy tertiary between orange and green.

sections.title: Name and meaning
sections.body:
*Citrine* began as a lemon-yellow word, and Paterson reports that the word kept that sense in France, while in English, by Maerz and Paul's reckoning, it came to share the meaning of *citron*, a browny yellow made by mixing green and orange [1]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930 dates the English color word to 1386 [2].

Dated to 1386, it is one of the older yellow words in English, and one that has moved [2]. Today's dictionaries, as St Clair's glossary shows, give it as the tertiary color between orange and green [3]. The swatch on this page is a different thing again: a vivid greenish yellow, nearer the lemon of the original meaning than the olive-brown of the later one [4].

sections.title: The tertiary citrine
sections.body:
The English tertiary sense comes through George Field, the London color maker and author of *Chromatography* (1835), named citrine, russet and olive as his three tertiary colors [5]. He made pigments for all three himself, so that every hue on his published scale existed as a real paint [5].

Field described a citrine color as an orange broken with green, which is why he could call his citrine lake a fine, transparent color that was rarely a true brown [6]. The lake was based on quercitron, a yellow dye from the bark of the quercitron oak, and later authors such as Salter (1869) treated it as the same pigment as brown pink [6]. Salter also described a "citrine brown" made from chromium compounds, which the Pigment Compendium notes had not become a commercial paint [7].

In Google Books the adjective use of the word, which is the color sense, peaks in the 1860s [8]. That is a generation after Field's *Chromatography* of 1835 [5][6].

Books therefore disagree about what color citrine is. Paterson's lemon, Field's broken orange-green, and the modern tertiary are three different places on the wheel [1][3][6].

sections.title: The stone
sections.body:
Citrine is also the yellow quartz. Quartz is silicon dioxide, usually colorless or white, and its colored varieties owe their hue to impurities: citrine to iron compounds, amethyst to iron in another state, rose quartz to titanium or fine rutile needles [9]. [[gem:amethyst|Amethyst]] is the same mineral with its iron changed by natural radiation, a different state of the same element [9][10].

In Sri Lanka, Finlay was shown "pineapple" citrines laid out beside lemon-colored topazes [11]. Paterson's list of birthstones gives citrine as an alternative to [[gem:topaz|topaz]] for November [12].

The ancient stones are less certain. Finlay's survey of the Hebrew Bible's breastplate stones records that Tharshish has been translated as green jasper or as citrine [13]. That is a translation question, not a record of the gem as we know it.

sections.title: In the alchemists' sequence
sections.body:
Medieval alchemy gave citrine a place in its sequence of color stages. Jarman's survey of alchemical color describes a stage of yellowing, *xanthosis* in the Greek texts, and quotes the formula in which the adept speaks of the citrine of the red [14]. Gage cites a fifteenth-century poem by Sir George Ripley in which citrine appears among the colors that must pass before the perfect white and the final red [15].

The word here is a stage in a process, not a hue to match. Gage uses the poem to show an area of experience where naming colors precisely was always essential, because the operator had to know when to proceed [15].

sections.title: The swatch is not the history
sections.body:
The color shown here, `#E4D00A`, is ISCC-NBS block 106, a vivid greenish yellow, and it sits within CIEDE2000 3.4 of the block's center [4]. Ridgway's *Color Standards* (1912), plate IV hue 21, gives a much darker olive-brown for citrine, though our copy is a scan of an aged plate and approximate [4].

So the two historical senses pull in opposite directions. The Ridgway plate and Field's broken orange-green fit the brown-citrine tradition, while this page's swatch fits the lemon sense and the gemstone [1][4][6]. The nearest named neighbor of the swatch in our data is [[lemon-yellow]], at 14 ΔE units [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, only 6 paintings carry this swatch at 5 percent of the canvas or more, about 0.03 percent [16]. It is rarer than 72 percent of the named colors [16]. Where it appears it plays an accent, never a mass of color [16].

It peaks in the 1900s, found in 0.4 percent of the 1,674 paintings we hold from that century, which is 5.9 times the rate the same museums would predict [16]. The earliest dated painting is from about 1700 [16]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue, not a pigment test, and six paintings is a small number [16].

To look for it, hold a piece of lemon quartz beside a true lemon and a gold ring, and notice how the greenish pull makes citrine the coolest of the three.
